fixes.find: Three: combustion venting, gas line size and power service. A gas-fired unit on an undersized or shared vent is a carbon monoxide risk. Illinois covers alarms through the Carbon Monoxide Alarm Detector Act. A gas line that cannot carry the added load is the same kind of risk. Rigging is the other hazard, since a unit has to reach a roof or a mechanical room safely. Venting deserves a check on any furnace work. NATE-certified technicians test every safety before the system is signed over.
fixes.replace: Three: combustion venting, gas line size and power service. A gas-fired unit on an undersized or shared vent can create a carbon monoxide risk. A gas line that cannot carry the added load is a related risk. Rigging is the other hazard, since a unit has to reach a roof or a mechanical room safely. If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds or anyone smells gas, everyone should leave the building first. Call 911, or the gas utility for a gas odor, from outside. Illinois has a carbon monoxide alarm law; which spaces it covers depends on the building. The proposal should list the startup safety tests, who performs them and how results are recorded before the system is signed over.
fixes.why: CRITICAL faq: replace 'NATE-certified technicians test every safety' with commissioning items for the proposal; add leave-and-call-911 safety step; qualify CO law

fixes.find: Uneven is the normal case. A south-facing storefront and an inside meeting room rarely want the same airflow. One thermostat in the wrong spot makes every other area wrong. Zoning splits a space into areas with separate control. That can mean more than one unit, dampers on one system, or separate indoor heads. Zones work best when they follow how the space is used through the day, with the controls set to match. Settling zones before the install costs far less than adding them later. The commercial HVAC range covers both.

City & Suburban prices upfront, with no hidden fees.
